voiceover.text: So, how does technology improve training, and how can we tell? A distance runner improves their personal best by two per cent in a season. That season they switched to a new type of racing shoe, trained on a newly resurfaced track, wore a GPS watch showing their pace in real time, and did the same training program as the year before. Write down how much of the improvement you'd credit to each of the four. Then the hard part: what evidence would you need to separate them, and does anyone have it?

scenes.title: three categories: what does it act on?

voiceover.text: The syllabus splits technology into three, and they act on different things. Training innovations change how training is delivered: virtual reality game scenarios, altitude or heat chambers, video analysis of an opponent, devices that resist or assist movement. They let athletes practise things that would be impossible, unsafe or too costly for real. Equipment advances act on the performance itself: shoes, track and pool surfaces, swimwear, bikes, protective gear. They change the mechanics directly. That includes assistive devices, like a running blade or an audible ball, which can decide whether someone competes at all. And recording and monitoring, like GPS units, heart rate monitors and video, act on the information coaches decide with. Monitoring doesn't make anyone faster. It improves decisions, and better decisions improve performance.

scenes.title: equipment, and where the line is drawn

voiceover.text: Equipment works through the biomechanics from earlier. A shoe or track that returns more of the energy stored at each foot strike lowers the cost of the same speed: efficiency. Swimwear, bike position and clothing cut drag, which matters more the faster you go. Assistive devices improve force application, and above all, access. But equipment is also where sport draws a line, and the line is hard to place, because every generation's gear improves on the last. Governing bodies have restricted equipment when they judged it gave too big an edge. Three questions usually decide it. How big is the advantage? Is it available to everyone, or only to well-funded athletes? And does it change what the sport is testing? If the equipment supplies the performance instead of the athlete, people call it technological doping.

scenes.title: monitoring: more data isn't more information

voiceover.text: Monitoring changed training more than anything else, because it made invisible things countable. A GPS unit records distance, high-speed running and accelerations. Over weeks, that becomes a load chart: daily bars that bounce around, and a trend underneath. But four limits matter. First, validity and reliability, from earlier. Each device works out its numbers its own way, so two brands can give different values for one session. Compare within one system, and trust the trend. Second, it measures what's easy. Distance is easy to count. Decision-making and how an athlete feels are not, and what gets measured gets managed, so training drifts toward the numbers. Third, numbers shouldn't override what a coach can see. And fourth, privacy. Location and body data are personal, so for school-age athletes, consent and who holds the data matter.

scenes.title: access: a multiplier, not a substitute

voiceover.text: Most of this assumes the technology is available, and for most athletes it isn't. A professional squad has GPS for everyone, analysts and environmental chambers. A school team has a phone camera and a free app. Here's the pattern. Technology gives its biggest returns where the basics are already maxed out, because then a tiny edge is all that's left. At school and community level, what limits performance is sleep, food, turning up and basic coaching, and technology doesn't fix those. So it's the same message as the recovery pyramid. Technology is a multiplier, not a substitute.

The verb is examine, and the hardest judgement is cause. Back to the runner. Four things changed together, and one of them, another year of training, is easy to forget. Different evidence answers different questions. One athlete improving shows they improved, not why. Many athletes improving after a technology spreads shows something changed, but the best-funded athletes adopt first, so that's not proof. A controlled comparison of the same athletes with and without it shows the effect's size, the strongest evidence. And a lab measure of energy cost shows the mechanism is real, not that it wins races. So an examine answer runs: the category, the mechanism, the evidence, the limits including access, then a judgement: for whom, when, and instead of what.
Two things to remember. Ask whether it acts on the training, the performance, or the decision. And technology is a multiplier, not a substitute.

scenes.title: attempt one (a vision app and smart insoles)

voiceover.text: Two exam questions. First. A vision-training app flashes numbers at the edge of a screen to train a goalkeeper's peripheral reactions. And a running squad wears pressure-sensing insoles that report each runner's foot-strike pattern after every session. For each, name the category, explain how it could improve performance, and state its most serious limitation. Pause here to answer.

The vision app is a training innovation. It gives many more reaction repetitions, but it may not transfer, because a screen isn't a real ball or real cues. The insoles are monitoring. They improve technique decisions. Their limits include device validity and measuring only what's easy. The classic mistake is saying the insoles make runners faster.

scenes.title: attempt two (shoes for the whole team?)

voiceover.text: Second. A school athletics team is deciding whether to buy expensive energy-return racing shoes for every runner. Examine this decision. Pause here to answer.

The shoes are an equipment advance. They return more energy each stride, lowering the cost of a given pace, so a real but small gain. But at school level, sleep, consistent training and coaching limit performance far more, and the budget could fund those. So, a multiplier: worth it for already well-prepared runners, not instead of the basics. The classic mistake is judging only whether the shoes work.

So name what the technology acts on, give its mechanism, weigh the evidence and the access, and judge it for this athlete, instead of what else. Watch this load chart. For weeks it tracks the trend. Then one week spikes to about twice the usual load, and an athlete gets hurt. How are injuries classified, and can the player go back on?
